name: libhv
workload: pingpong echo-servers benchmark: 4 threads, 1000 connections, 10s run, TCP echo, measuring aggregate read throughput (MB/s)
claimed_speedup: libhv 215 MB/s vs libevent 157 MB/s (~1.37x) and vs libuv 156 MB/s (~1.38x); also beats asio (132 MB/s) and Poco (165 MB/s), trails libev (210 MB/s)
tradeoffs: Simpler, richer-protocol API than libevent/libuv/asio (built-in HTTP/WebSocket/MQTT/Redis); C core with C++ wrapper (evpp namespace, unrelated to Qihoo360/evpp)
caveats: Numbers come from the project's own echo-servers/ harness run on GitHub Actions CI; compiler flags and exact CPU model are not stated in the README, only that results are reproducible via ./echo-servers/benchmark.sh; margin over libevent/libuv is modest (~37-38%) and libhv trails libev.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:event-loop -> ithewei/libhv -> repos/ithewei/libhv/readme

name: PhotonLibOS
workload: TCP ping-pong test (1,000 connections, 512-byte buffers) and streaming test (4 connections, 512-byte buffers), measuring per-core QPS and bandwidth
claimed_speedup: Ping-pong: Photon 412K QPS / 1.57 Gb/s vs boost::asio 393K QPS / 1.49 Gb/s (~1.05x); streaming: Photon 1,604K QPS / 6.12 Gb/s vs boost::asio 634K QPS / 2.42 Gb/s (~2.5x)
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build type (exact compiler/optimization flags not stated)
hardware: 64-core Intel Xeon Platinum @ 2.70GHz, 128GB RAM, 32Gb NIC, Linux kernel 6.x
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars; used in production at Alibaba, Ant Group, ByteDance, Xiaomi, XSKY (e.g. overlaybd, OSSFSv2)
tradeoffs: Stackful-coroutine model; also compares against cocoyaxi, tokio, monoio, Go, libco and others on the same page (Photon leads on per-core QPS in both tests)
caveats: First-party benchmark; hardware CPU model is stated but exact compiler and optimization flags are not, only that it's a CMake Release build; benchmark source is linked (examples/perf/net-perf.cpp) but was not independently re-run here.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/alibaba/PhotonLibOS/readme -> linked performance docs page

name: UCall
baseline: FastAPI/uvicorn (Python, asyncio - typically epoll-based event loop on Linux)
workload: JSON-RPC round-trip: single-client latency and 32-client throughput on AWS c7g.metal (Graviton3), Ubuntu 22.10, Linux kernel 5.19
claimed_speedup: UCall with io_uring (C): 22us latency / 231,000 rps vs FastAPI over REST: 1,203us / 3,184 rps (~55x latency, ~72x throughput); vs FastAPI over WebSocket: 86us / 11,356 rps (~3.9x latency, ~20x throughput)
hardware: AWS c7g.metal, Graviton 3, Ubuntu 22.10, Linux kernel 5.19
tradeoffs: Cross-language comparison (C/io_uring server vs Python/ASGI client stack), so the headline numbers conflate io_uring efficiency with Python interpreter/framework overhead
caveats: The FastAPI comparison is cross-language and not a controlled same-codebase event-loop shootout. A cleaner internal comparison exists in the same table: UCall's own 'POSIX' backend (src/engine_posix.cpp, blocking per-thread accept/recv, not epoll) does 62us/79,000 rps vs UCall's io_uring backend (src/engine_uring.cpp) at 22us/231,000 rps (~2.8x), but that baseline is blocking sockets, not epoll, so it was not used as the primary claim.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:io-uring -> unum-cloud/UCall; corroborated via HN Algolia ("Show HN: Faster FastAPI with simdjson and io_uring", 290 points)

name: aquatic (aquatic_udp)
baseline: epoll (opentracker, a widely-deployed epoll-based UDP BitTorrent tracker; aquatic_udp's own mio/epoll backend is also compared)
workload: UDP BitTorrent tracker load test (aquatic_bencher, --cpu-mode subsequent-one-per-pair) at 1-16 CPU cores, measuring average responses/second, best result
claimed_speedup: At 16 cores: aquatic_udp (io_uring) 2,258,321 rps vs opentracker (epoll, C) 1,645,828 rps (~1.37x) and vs aquatic_udp's own mio/epoll backend 2,037,713 rps (~1.11x); at 1 core: io_uring 226,065 vs opentracker 190,540 (~1.19x) vs mio/epoll 186,939 (~1.21x)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.76.0, GCC 12.2.0 (for opentracker/chihaya); optimization flags not itemized beyond default release builds
hardware: Hetzner CCX63: 48 dedicated vCPUs, AMD EPYC 7003 (Milan), Debian 12.4, Linux 6.5.10
stars_or_usage: 622 stars; explodie.org public tracker (opentracker) reports serving ~100,000 req/s in production for comparison
tradeoffs: aquatic_udp is Rust (not C++); io_uring backend requires a recent Linux kernel; opentracker and chihaya are separately maintained C/Go projects benchmarked at pinned commits
caveats: Chihaya (Go) trails all others by ~10x and is likely not representative of Go's ceiling; benchmark authored by the aquatic maintainer (not fully independent), though opentracker/chihaya are third-party competing implementations.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:io-uring -> greatest-ape/aquatic -> documents/aquatic-udp-load-test-2024-02-10.md

name: uWebSockets (µWebSockets / uSockets)
workload: HTTP requests/second on a fanless Raspberry Pi 4, compared to Node.js (per README, linking to an external blog post)
claimed_speedup: "12x the HTTP requests per second as compared to Node.js"
stars_or_usage: 19k stars; used by major crypto exchanges handling billions of USD/day in trade volume
tradeoffs: uSockets (the underlying eventing layer) supports five event-loop backends including libuv, ASIO, GCD and raw epoll/kqueue, so libuv is also an optional backend, not just a competitor; header-only C++17 built on a C core
caveats: The linked source blog post (levelup.gitconnected.com) returned HTTP 403 and could not be opened this session, so the '12x' figure is only verified as appearing in the uWebSockets README/READMORE.md, not independently confirmed at the source with full methodology; the main README also states 'Intellectual property, all rights reserved' alongside the Apache-2.0 notice, creating some licensing ambiguity despite GitHub detecting Apache-2.0.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/uNetworking/uWebSockets/readme -> benchmarks/README.md and misc/READMORE.md

name: monoio
workload: Extreme-performance TCP test on ByteDance production network: fixed number of client connections against 4 server cores / 16 client cores, 1KB messages, comparing io_uring (Monoio), io_uring (Glommio) and epoll (Tokio) runtimes
claimed_speedup: Monoio peak ~810,075 QPS vs Tokio (epoll) peak ~434,565 QPS (~1.86x) and vs Glommio (io_uring) peak ~603,016 QPS (~1.34x) at 4 server cores
compiler_and_flags: rust nightly-2021-11-26 (build optimization flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz, Intel X710 10GbE NIC, Linux 5.15.4-arch1-1
tradeoffs: Thread-per-core, non-Send/Sync design (values do not escape thread on await); at very low connection counts on a single core, Monoio's io_uring submission latency is higher than Tokio's epoll path, so Tokio wins that narrow case
caveats: First-party benchmark authored by the Monoio maintainers, not an independent suite, though hardware, kernel and rust toolchain versions are stated and raw numeric data is published; test dates from late 2021 on an early io_uring-era kernel (5.15), so results may not reflect current io_uring/epoll performance.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:io-uring -> bytedance/monoio -> docs/en/benchmark.md -> raw_data.txt

name: io_uring-echo-server (frevib)
workload: TCP echo server requests/second vs number of concurrent clients (1-1000) and message sizes (128/512/1000 bytes), using the rust_echo_bench load generator, comparing a minimal io_uring (IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL) echo server against a minimal epoll echo server by the same author
claimed_speedup: 128-byte messages: io_uring peaks at 216,637 req/s (300 clients) vs epoll peak 152,561 req/s (150 clients), ~1.4x; at 1000 clients: io_uring 173,343 vs epoll 108,380 req/s, ~1.6x
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark client (rust_echo_bench) built with `cargo run --release`; the C echo servers are built with `make` and server-side compiler flags are not stated
hardware: MacBook Pro 6-core 2.6GHz host running a VMware Ubuntu 18.04 guest with 6 vCPUs (3 physical cores), 2 cores isolated via isolcpus for the echo server, Linux 5.6.0-rc1+ with IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL
stars_or_usage: 400 stars; widely cited as a reference io_uring-vs-epoll benchmark (referenced on Hacker News/Twitter)
tradeoffs: At the time of writing, the io_uring echo server needed a per-connection buffer indexed by file descriptor number (segfault risk at high fd counts) and became unresponsive under sustained load with >2000 clients; the epoll counterpart did not show these issues
caveats: Both implementations were written by the same author (not a fully independent third party) specifically to isolate epoll vs io_uring; exact CPU model and C-side compiler flags are not stated; the benchmark is from 2020 on an early io_uring kernel patch (5.6.0-rc1+, pre-mainline IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL), so it may not reflect current io_uring/liburing performance.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:io-uring -> frevib/io_uring-echo-server README -> benchmarks/benchmarks.md; corroborated via HN Algolia ("io_uring vs epoll: echo server benchmarks")
